notes.meaning: Jesus continued His ministry in Galilee rather than Judea. The religious leaders in Judea were actively plotting to kill Him after He healed a man on the Sabbath. He did not avoid Judea out of fear, but because the right time for His arrest had not yet arrived.

The Feast of Tabernacles was an annual autumn harvest festival in Jerusalem. Jewish families built and lived in small shelters made of branches for seven days to remember how God cared for Israel in the wilderness after the exodus from Egypt. It was one of the major feasts that Jewish men were expected to attend.

Jesus' brothers urged Him to leave Galilee and go down to Judea. They wanted Him to perform His miracles openly in Jerusalem so that His followers could see them. Their words sounded encouraging, but they came from worldly thinking and a lack of true faith in Him.

His brothers argued that anyone who wants to be famous does not hide away in small Galilean towns. They thought that if He was truly performing miracles, He should show Himself to the world at the feast in the capital city. They assumed that Jesus sought the same earthly applause and attention that ordinary men crave.

Even Jesus' own family members did not believe in Him as the Messiah at this stage of His ministry. Although they had seen His extraordinary deeds, they doubted His divine claims and mission. Later, after His resurrection, they came to true faith and joined the early believers in Jerusalem.

Jesus told them that His appointed time had not yet come. Every step of His life was guided by God's timetable, especially His public entrance into Jerusalem and His road to the cross. His brothers could go whenever they wished because they were not under the same divine mission.

The unbelieving world had no reason to hate Jesus' brothers, because their attitudes and values matched the world around them. But the world hated Jesus because He openly exposed its sin and told people the truth about their evil deeds. Telling people the truth about their wrongdoing often stirs up anger.

Jesus told His brothers to go ahead to the feast without Him. He was not going up with their public pilgrim caravan because God's appointed time for Him to arrive had not yet come. He did not say He would never attend, but that He would not go for the sake of public display.

After giving His brothers this answer, Jesus remained behind in Galilee. He waited quietly for a few days while the large traveling crowds departed. He did not act on impulse or human pressure, but stayed in line with God's timing.

Once His brothers and the festival crowds had left, Jesus also traveled up to Jerusalem. He made the journey quietly and privately rather than with a large caravan. This prevented an early public stir and avoided unnecessary conflict with the authorities before His work was done.

The Jewish religious leaders were watching for Jesus at the festival. They kept asking where He was, expecting Him to arrive because Jewish law called every man to attend. Their search was not friendly; they were waiting for an opportunity to confront and arrest Him.

The crowds attending the feast whispered about Jesus among themselves and were sharply divided. Some thought He was a good and upright man whose deeds helped people. Others insisted He was a dangerous deceiver who was leading the nation astray.

No one in the crowd dared to speak about Jesus out in the open. The rulers had created an atmosphere of fear, and people worried about being punished or expelled from the community. Those who had good things to say about Him kept their opinions strictly private.

When the eight-day festival was about halfway through, Jesus entered the temple courts and began to teach publicly. The initial excitement about His arrival had settled, making it a good time to proclaim the truth. He boldly took up His role as a teacher right in the heart of Jerusalem.

The leaders and crowds were astonished by Jesus' deep understanding of the sacred Scriptures. They knew He had never studied in the official rabbinical schools or sat under famous teachers. Instead of receiving what He taught, they questioned how an untrained man could know so much.

Jesus answered their astonishment by explaining that His teaching was not His own human invention. He had not devised it by Himself, but had received it directly from God the Father who sent Him. He was speaking as God's true messenger, delivering heaven's message.

Anyone who truly desires to do the will of God will recognize whether Jesus' message comes from heaven or from human imagination. True spiritual understanding begins with a heart that is ready to obey God. Those who honestly want to please God will see the divine truth in what Jesus says.

A teacher who invents his own message usually does it to win human applause and personal glory. In contrast, someone who seeks only to honor the God who sent him is completely truthful. Because Jesus sought only His Father's honor, there was no deceit or falsehood in Him.

Jesus pointed out that although Moses gave them God's law, none of them actually kept it. They boasted of their loyalty to the law, yet they were breaking it by plotting to murder Him. Their claim to be defenders of Moses was exposed as pure hypocrisy.

People in the crowd reacted angrily and accused Jesus of having a demon, meaning He was crazy or out of His mind. Many of these visiting pilgrims knew nothing about the secret plots of the rulers in Jerusalem. They thought Jesus was imagining threats that did not exist.

Jesus answered by reminding them of the miracle He had worked on His previous visit to Jerusalem, when He healed a paralyzed man at the pool of Bethesda. Everyone had been shocked because He performed that healing on a Sabbath. That single act of mercy was the real reason the rulers wanted Him dead.

Jesus reminded them that Moses instructed them to circumcise baby boys on the eighth day, a practice that actually began centuries earlier with Abraham. If that eighth day happened to be a Sabbath, Jewish priests still carried out the rite. They rightly recognized that keeping this covenant duty took priority over resting on the Sabbath.

Jesus showed that if circumcision is allowed on the Sabbath to keep the law, there is no reason to be furious with Him for healing an entire person on that day. Carrying out an outward covenant sign was accepted work, so making a suffering man whole was even more fitting. God's purpose for the Sabbath was never meant to stop acts of mercy.

Jesus told them to stop judging by superficial outward appearances and to start judging with true fairness. On the surface, healing on the Sabbath might have seemed like a violation of the rest day, but it fulfilled God's desire for compassion. We must always look at God's heart rather than judging others by hasty impressions.

Some of the residents who lived in Jerusalem recognized Jesus and began to ask if He was the man the authorities were trying to kill. Unlike the visitors from out of town, the city dwellers were familiar with the rulers' murderous plots. They were surprised to see Him standing right before them in the temple.

The people were amazed that Jesus was speaking openly and that the authorities were doing nothing to silence Him. They wondered aloud whether the rulers had secretly changed their minds and realized that He was indeed the promised Christ. God held back the enemies of Jesus so He could finish delivering His message.
